{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_a7e399ba2392470c852ff2ea","type":"tool_result","content":"0\t# hetzner-auction-dashboard Plan\n1\t\n2\t_Last updated: 2026-08-01._ This plan and its companion docs (`docs/research/existing-tools.md`, `docs/notes/benchmark-priority.md`) are living references — if this date and either of those drift more than a few weeks apart, treat the older one as stale and reconcile before trusting it.\n3\t\n4\t## Overview\n5\t\n6\tA fully static, client-side dashboard for browsing Hetzner's dedicated server auction. A separate scheduled pipeline fetches auction listings, enriches each one with a CPU benchmark score and derived cost-efficiency metrics, and publishes the result as a single flat Parquet file. The browser loads that Parquet file directly into DuckDB-WASM and does all search/filtering/sorting locally via SQL — there is no client-side join and no per-request backend API. Success looks like: reaching for this dashboard instead of Hetzner's own auction page whenever deal-hunting, because it shows the same listings ranked by real value — price per benchmark point — instead of raw price alone.\n7\t\n8\t## Competitive Positioning\n9\t\n10\tPer `docs/research/existing-tools.md`: joining a CPU benchmark score onto live auction listings is **not a novel idea** — three existing tools (Auction Browser+, hzfind, Server Auction Tracker) already do it, all sourcing PassMark exclusively. The category leader on every other axis, **Server Radar** (366 stars, actively maintained, SvelteKit + DuckDB-WASM — architecturally the closest sibling to this project), has **no** benchmark integration at all.\n11\t\n12\tAlso worth naming, though it's not a benchmark-joining competitor: **hetzner-cli** (Robot API CLI/library, not a web dashboard) has the widest raw filter/sort field coverage found in the survey — 11 sort keys, including a numeric bandwidth-minimum filter — and zero benchmark integration of its own. It's cited elsewhere in this plan (Benchmark Strategy, Data Models) as the precedent for filter/sort field design, not as competition on the benchmark join.\n13\t\n14\tThe gap isn't \"does a benchmark score exist\" — it's that nobody has paired good benchmark data with sustained maintenance and feature depth. Concretely, every existing implementation has one of these weaknesses:\n15\t\n16\t1. Single-source (PassMark only), unverified/incomplete CPU coverage (~90 models at best, disclosed by only one tool).\n17\t2. Opaque fixed-weight blended scores (Auction Browser+, Server Auction Tracker) that hide the number that actually matters instead of exposing it directly.\n18\t3. No performance-normalized history or alerting — every price-history feature found (Server Radar) tracks raw €, not €-per-benchmark-point over time.\n19\t4. No workload weighting — nothing lets a user favor single-thread vs. multi-thread performance for their own use case.\n20\t\n21\tThis project's differentiation, in priority order: **(a)** treat the benchmark join itself as the core deliverable and keep it accurate and well-covered (unmatched CPUs surfaced, not silently dropped or guessed — see Benchmark Strategy), **(b)** expose value as separate, transparent per-resource metrics rather than one opaque blended score, **(c)** leave room to grow into Server-Radar-grade breadth (history, alerts) later without having to re-architect, since v1 deliberately does not compete on that axis yet.\n22\t\n23\t## What It Is NOT\n24\t\n25\t- **Not a price-alert/notification bot.** No push notifications, email, or webhooks in v1 — performance-normalized alerting is a named v2 candidate, gated on the historical-stats work landing first.\n26\t- **Not a marketplace or reseller.** This never buys, holds, or resells servers, and never wraps Hetzner's checkout flow. It's a read-only view over data Hetzner already publishes; ordering still happens on Hetzner's own site.\n27\t- **Not a general-purpose CPU benchmark database.** `benchmark-map/` exists only to answer \"what's this Hetzner auction listing's CPU worth\" — it only ever contains CPUs that have actually appeared in the auction feed, not a standalone PassMark mirror.\n28\t- **Not a client-side join.** The browser never computes or looks up a benchmark score at query time — it only filters/sorts a column already joined server-side into the Parquet file (see Benchmark Strategy). If a future UI change ever seems to need a lookup against `benchmark-map/` in the browser, that's a signal the pipeline is missing a precomputed field, not a signal to add a join client-side.\n29\t\n30\t## Acceptance Scenarios\n31\t\n32\t### Scenario 1: Happy Path — Filter by CPU Family + RAM\n33\t**Setup:** Pipeline has published a current Parquet snapshot; the dashboard is loaded in a browser.\n34\t**Action:** User sets a CPU-family filter (e.g. \"Ryzen\") and a minimum-RAM filter (e.g. ≥64GB), leaving everything else at defaults.\n35\t**Expected:** Results show only matching listings, sorted by `price_per_benchmark_point_multi` ascending with `NULLS FIRST` (the default sort); any listing with `benchmark_matched = false` has a NULL `price_per_benchmark_point_multi` (and NULL `price_per_benchmark_point_single`) and therefore sorts to the top of the results, visibly flagged as unscored rather than blended in at the bottom or omitted.\n36\t**Pass criteria:**\n37\t- Filtered set matches only listings satisfying both filters\n38\t- Default sort order is `price_per_benchmark_point_multi` ascending, `NULLS FIRST`\n39\t- Unscored listings appear with an explicit \"unscored\" indicator, grouped at the top of the results, never blank or omitted\n40\t**Fail criteria:**\n41\t- An unscored listing is silently dropped from results\n42\t- Default sort is raw price instead of `price_per_benchmark_point_multi`\n43\t- Unscored listings sort to the bottom of the results (NULLS LAST) or are scattered among scored listings instead of grouped at the top\n44\t\n45\t### Scenario 2: Degraded — Hetzner Feed Unreachable\n46\t**Setup:** A scheduled 10-minute pipeline run starts; Hetzner's auction feed endpoint times out or errors.\n47\t**Action:** Pipeline attempts its normal fetch → normalize → compute → publish cycle.\n48\t**Expected:** Pipeline aborts before touching the live Parquet key in R2 (see Pipeline Run Lifecycle); the previously published snapshot keeps serving unchanged; the failure is logged.\n49\t**Pass criteria:**\n50\t- Live R2 key is byte-identical to before the failed run\n51\t- Dashboard continues to load and query the last-known-good snapshot\n52\t- Failure is logged with enough detail to diagnose (endpoint, status/error, timestamp)\n53\t**Fail criteria:**\n54\t- Live key is partially overwritten or corrupted\n55\t- Dashboard shows broken/empty results because of an upstream failure it had no part in\n56\t\n57\t### Scenario 3: Degraded — Client Parquet/DuckDB-WASM Load Failure\n58\t**Setup:** Dashboard loads in a browser; the Parquet fetch via DuckDB-WASM httpfs fails (network error, CORS misconfiguration, or WASM init failure).\n59\t**Action:** User opens the dashboard normally.\n60\t**Expected:** Dashboard shows a plain error state naming the likely cause (see Graceful Degradation), instead of a blank page or silent hang.\n61\t**Pass criteria:**\n62\t- An explicit error message is shown, never a blank/frozen UI\n63\t- No stale or partial data is rendered as if it were current\n64\t**Fail criteria:**\n65\t- Blank page with no indication anything went wrong\n66\t- Partial/garbled data rendered without an error indicator\n67\t\n68\t### Scenario 4: Success Metrics\n69\t- **Performance:** `[FILL IN once real data volume is known — see Performance Ceiling]`. Rough expectation is sub-second initial query time and near-instant re-filter/re-sort on a typical current-auction-sized snapshot, since DuckDB-WASM's range requests only fetch the row groups a query touches.\n70\t- **Functionality:** v1 supports every filter/sort listed in Client Dashboard Scope (v1) against a live, benchmark-joined snapshot, with correct staleness display and unscored-listing flagging. History, alerts, and comparison view are explicitly not required for v1.\n71\t- **Adoption:** the one signal that matters for a solo tool — checking this dashboard instead of opening Hetzner's own Server Auction page directly when deal-hunting. Catching myself opening Hetzner's page out of habit within the first month is a sign the dashboard isn't pulling its weight yet.\n72\t\n73\t## Architecture\n74\t\n75\tTwo independent halves connected only by a Parquet file:\n76\t\n77\t### 1. Pipeline (server-side, scheduled)\n78\t\n79\t- Fetches current listings from Hetzner's public Server Auction data feed every **10 minutes**. Hetzner doesn't document a fixed update schedule (price drops happen at randomized intervals by design), so this matches the practical cadence third-party tools converge on — frequent enough to catch price drops and new listings without hammering the endpoint.\n80\t- Normalizes each listing's free-text CPU name and matches it against a maintained CPU benchmark reference table (see Benchmark Strategy). Matching is fuzzy/alias-based with a manual-override list for CPUs that don't match cleanly — this is the part expected to need ongoing curation, not the dashboard code itself.\n81\t- Computes derived cost fields for every listing: effective total monthly cost (`price_effective_monthly`, folding in the setup fee — see Data Models for the formula), then price per benchmark point — single-thread and multi-thread computed and stored separately, never blended (see ADR-3) — price per GB RAM, and price per TB disk (see Data Models for each formula).\n82\t- Writes ONE denormalized Parquet file — no relational structure, every column a query might filter/sort on is already present.\n83\t- Publishes the Parquet file to **Cloudflare R2** (native CORS + HTTP range-request support, required for DuckDB-WASM to do partial reads instead of downloading the whole file on every page load). Chosen over self-hosting on Garage/SeaweedFS to avoid standing up public HTTPS ingress for what's otherwise a personal tool, and it matches Server Radar's proven architecture for this exact use case. Requires an R2 API token stored as a cluster secret (OpenBao/ExternalSecret, matching existing patterns) for the pipeline to push to.\n84\t- Runs as a long-lived Deployment with an internal refresh loop (house rule: no Job/CronJob) on a Rackspace Spot cluster, wired through GitOps (`jedarden/declarative-config`, `k8s/` path) — never a live kubectl mutation. Compute (pipeline) and hosting (R2/Pages) are intentionally decoupled: the cluster only needs egress to Cloudflare's API, nothing is served from cluster ingress.\n85\t- **Format verification.** Before the pipeline depends on it in production, the chosen Parquet writer's output is confirmed compatible with DuckDB-WASM's httpfs range-request reads via the conformance test in Testing Strategy — checked once by the end of Phase 3 (see Phase 3 completion criteria and Testing Strategy), not re-verified every run and not deferred to Phase 4 or 5.\n86\t- **Operational visibility.** The pipeline logs the timestamp of its last successful publish, so a stalled pipeline is visible without needing the dashboard open — the same `fetched_at` value the client already surfaces as a staleness indicator, just also checked from the pipeline side.\n87\t\n88\t### Pipeline Run Lifecycle\n89\t\n90\tEvery run — the v1 current-snapshot Parquet file, its companion `unmatched-cpus.json` unmatched-CPU report (see Benchmark Strategy), and later each v2 history file — follows the same verify-before-publish discipline (steps 1-5 below), so one failure mode and one fix covers all three. Step 6's specific \"promote, then clean up\" mechanics differ slightly for history files, since they never reuse a key — see that step for the scoping:\n91\t\n92\t1. **Fetch** — pull current listings from Hetzner's auction feed.\n93\t2. **Normalize/match** — clean CPU strings, resolve against `benchmark-map/`, flag unmatched.\n94\t3. **Compute** — derive `price_effective_monthly` first (see Data Models for the setup-fee formula), then `price_per_benchmark_point_single`, `price_per_benchmark_point_multi`, `price_per_gb_ram`, `price_per_tb_disk` (see Data Models for each formula).\n95\t4. **Write to a temp key in R2** — never write directly to the live key the client reads. Set a short `Cache-Control: max-age=60` header on the object at write time (see ADR-4) — well under the 10-minute publish cadence, so any CDN staleness after the swap self-resolves quickly.\n96\t5. **Verify** — confirm the temp object is readable and structurally sane before it's allowed to become live: non-zero size, and parses as valid Parquet (for the snapshot/history files) or valid JSON (for the unmatched-CPU report).\n97\t6. **Promote temp key to its permanent key.** For the snapshot and the unmatched-CPU report — which reuse one fixed, well-known live key every run — this is an atomic swap: copy-then-delete-old, since R2/S3-compatible storage has no native rename; the old key is only deleted after the new one is confirmed in place. A v2 history file instead writes to a brand-new, never-before-used key each run (see Storage pattern for history), so there is no old key to delete — promotion there is just the temp-to-permanent-key copy, confirmed in place, with nothing to clean up after. Either way, the `Cache-Control` header carries through to the live/permanent key.\n98\t7. **On failure at any step** — abort immediately without touching the live key. No workload weighting — nothing lets a user favor single-thread vs. multi-thread performance for their own use case.\n\nThis project's differentiation, in priority order: **(a)** treat the benchmark join itself as the core deliverable and keep it accurate and well-covered (unmatched CPUs surfaced, not silently dropped or guessed — see Benchmark Strategy), **(b)** expose value as separate, transparent per-resource metrics rather than one opaque blended score, **(c)** leave room to grow into Server-Radar-grade breadth (history, alerts) later without having to re-architect, since v1 deliberately does not compete on that axis yet.\n\n## What It Is NOT\n\n- **Not a price-alert/notification bot.** No push notifications, email, or webhooks in v1 — performance-normalized alerting is a named v2 candidate, gated on the historical-stats work landing first.\n- **Not a marketplace or reseller.** This never buys, holds, or resells servers, and never wraps Hetzner's checkout flow. It's a read-only view over data Hetzner already publishes; ordering still happens on Hetzner's own site.\n- **Not a general-purpose CPU benchmark database.** `benchmark-map/` exists only to answer \"what's this Hetzner auction listing's CPU worth\" — it only ever contains CPUs that have actually appeared in the auction feed, not a standalone PassMark mirror.\n- **Not a client-side join.** The browser never computes or looks up a benchmark score at query time — it only filters/sorts a column already joined server-side into the Parquet file (see Benchmark Strategy). If a future UI change ever seems to need a lookup against `benchmark-map/` in the browser, that's a signal the pipeline is missing a precomputed field, not a signal to add a join client-side.\n\n## Acceptance Scenarios\n\n### Scenario 1: Happy Path — Filter by CPU Family + RAM\n**Setup:** Pipeline has published a current Parquet snapshot; the dashboard is loaded in a browser.\n**Action:** User sets a CPU-family filter (e.g. \"Ryzen\") and a minimum-RAM filter (e.g. ≥64GB), leaving everything else at defaults.\n**Expected:** Results show only matching listings, sorted by `price_per_benchmark_point_multi` ascending with `NULLS FIRST` (the default sort); any listing with `benchmark_matched = false` has a NULL `price_per_benchmark_point_multi` (and NULL `price_per_benchmark_point_single`) and therefore sorts to the top of the results, visibly flagged as unscored rather than blended in at the bottom or omitted.\n**Pass criteria:**\n- Filtered set matches only listings satisfying both filters\n- Default sort order is `price_per_benchmark_point_multi` ascending, `NULLS FIRST`\n- Unscored listings appear with an explicit \"unscored\" indicator, grouped at the top of the results, never blank or omitted\n**Fail criteria:**\n- An unscored listing is silently dropped from results\n- Default sort is raw price instead of `price_per_benchmark_point_multi`\n- Unscored listings sort to the bottom of the results (NULLS LAST) or are scattered among scored listings instead of grouped at the top\n\n### Scenario 2: Degraded — Hetzner Feed Unreachable\n**Setup:** A scheduled 10-minute pipeline run starts; Hetzner's auction feed endpoint times out or errors.\n**Action:** Pipeline attempts its normal fetch → normalize → compute → publish cycle.\n**Expected:** Pipeline aborts before touching the live Parquet key in R2 (see Pipeline Run Lifecycle); the previously published snapshot keeps serving unchanged; the failure is logged.\n**Pass criteria:**\n- Live R2 key is byte-identical to before the failed run\n- Dashboard continues to load and query the last-known-good snapshot\n- Failure is logged with enough detail to diagnose (endpoint, status/error, timestamp)\n**Fail criteria:**\n- Live key is partially overwritten or corrupted\n- Dashboard shows broken/empty results because of an upstream failure it had no part in\n\n### Scenario 3: Degraded — Client Parquet/DuckDB-WASM Load Failure\n**Setup:** Dashboard loads in a browser; the Parquet fetch via DuckDB-WASM httpfs fails (network error, CORS misconfiguration, or WASM init failure).\n**Action:** User opens the dashboard normally.\n**Expected:** Dashboard shows a plain error state naming the likely cause (see Graceful Degradation), instead of a blank page or silent hang.\n**Pass criteria:**\n- An explicit error message is shown, never a blank/frozen UI\n- No stale or partial data is rendered as if it were current\n**Fail criteria:**\n- Blank page with no indication anything went wrong\n- Partial/garbled data rendered without an error indicator\n\n### Scenario 4: Success Metrics\n- **Performance:** `[FILL IN once real data volume is known — see Performance Ceiling]`. Rough expectation is sub-second initial query time and near-instant re-filter/re-sort on a typical current-auction-sized snapshot, since DuckDB-WASM's range requests only fetch the row groups a query touches.\n- **Functionality:** v1 supports every filter/sort listed in Client Dashboard Scope (v1) against a live, benchmark-joined snapshot, with correct staleness display and unscored-listing flagging. History, alerts, and comparison view are explicitly not required for v1.\n- **Adoption:** the one signal that matters for a solo tool — checking this dashboard instead of opening Hetzner's own Server Auction page directly when deal-hunting. Catching myself opening Hetzner's page out of habit within the first month is a sign the dashboard isn't pulling its weight yet.\n\n## Architecture\n\nTwo independent halves connected only by a Parquet file:\n\n### 1. Pipeline (server-side, scheduled)\n\n- Fetches current listings from Hetzner's public Server Auction data feed every **10 minutes**. Hetzner doesn't document a fixed update schedule (price drops happen at randomized intervals by design), so this matches the practical cadence third-party tools converge on — frequent enough to catch price drops and new listings without hammering the endpoint.\n- Normalizes each listing's free-text CPU name and matches it against a maintained CPU benchmark reference table (see Benchmark Strategy). Matching is fuzzy/alias-based with a manual-override list for CPUs that don't match cleanly — this is the part expected to need ongoing curation, not the dashboard code itself.\n- Computes derived cost fields for every listing: effective total monthly cost (`price_effective_monthly`, folding in the setup fee — see Data Models for the formula), then price per benchmark point — single-thread and multi-thread computed and stored separately, never blended (see ADR-3) — price per GB RAM, and price per TB disk (see Data Models for each formula).\n- Writes ONE denormalized Parquet file — no relational structure, every column a query might filter/sort on is already present.\n- Publishes the Parquet file to **Cloudflare R2** (native CORS + HTTP range-request support, required for DuckDB-WASM to do partial reads instead of downloading the whole file on every page load). Chosen over self-hosting on Garage/SeaweedFS to avoid standing up public HTTPS ingress for what's otherwise a personal tool, and it matches Server Radar's proven architecture for this exact use case. Requires an R2 API token stored as a cluster secret (OpenBao/ExternalSecret, matching existing patterns) for the pipeline to push to.\n- Runs as a long-lived Deployment with an internal refresh loop (house rule: no Job/CronJob) on a Rackspace Spot cluster, wired through GitOps (`jedarden/declarative-config`, `k8s/` path) — never a live kubectl mutation. Compute (pipeline) and hosting (R2/Pages) are intentionally decoupled: the cluster only needs egress to Cloudflare's API, nothing is served from cluster ingress.\n- **Format verification.** Before the pipeline depends on it in production, the chosen Parquet writer's output is confirmed compatible with DuckDB-WASM's httpfs range-request reads via the conformance test in Testing Strategy — checked once by the end of Phase 3 (see Phase 3 completion criteria and Testing Strategy), not re-verified every run and not deferred to Phase 4 or 5.\n- **Operational visibility.** The pipeline logs the timestamp of its last successful publish, so a stalled pipeline is visible without needing the dashboard open — the same `fetched_at` value the client already surfaces as a staleness indicator, just also checked from the pipeline side.\n\n### Pipeline Run Lifecycle\n\nEvery run — the v1 current-snapshot Parquet file, its companion `unmatched-cpus.json` unmatched-CPU report (see Benchmark Strategy), and later each v2 history file — follows the same verify-before-publish discipline (steps 1-5 below), so one failure mode and one fix covers all three. Step 6's specific \"promote, then clean up\" mechanics differ slightly for history files, since they never reuse a key — see that step for the scoping:\n\n1. **Fetch** — pull current listings from Hetzner's auction feed.\n2. **Normalize/match** — clean CPU strings, resolve against `benchmark-map/`, flag unmatched.\n3. **Compute** — derive `price_effective_monthly` first (see Data Models for the setup-fee formula), then `price_per_benchmark_point_single`, `price_per_benchmark_point_multi`, `price_per_gb_ram`, `price_per_tb_disk` (see Data Models for each formula).\n4. **Write to a temp key in R2** — never write directly to the live key the client reads. Set a short `Cache-Control: max-age=60` header on the object at write time (see ADR-4) — well under the 10-minute publish cadence, so any CDN staleness after the swap self-resolves quickly.\n5. **Verify** — confirm the temp object is readable and structurally sane before it's allowed to become live: non-zero size, and parses as valid Parquet (for the snapshot/history files) or valid JSON (for the unmatched-CPU report).\n6. **Promote temp key to its permanent key.** For the snapshot and the unmatched-CPU report — which reuse one fixed, well-known live key every run — this is an atomic swap: copy-then-delete-old, since R2/S3-compatible storage has no native rename; the old key is only deleted after the new one is confirmed in place. A v2 history file instead writes to a brand-new, never-before-used key each run (see Storage pattern for history), so there is no old key to delete — promotion there is just the temp-to-permanent-key copy, confirmed in place, with nothing to clean up after. Either way, the `Cache-Control` header carries through to the live/permanent key.\n7. **On failure at any step** — abort immediately without touching the live key. The previously published snapshot keeps serving untouched; the run is simply retried next cycle.\n","numLines":100,"startLine":0,"totalLines":378}}}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"call_7638d724effb4bafac09ce04","type":"tool_result","content":"200\t### Anti-Patterns Catalog\n201\t\n202\tConsolidating the \"deliberately do not\" decisions already scattered through this plan into one place:\n203\t\n204\t- **No blended benchmark score.** Hides the number that matters most behind an arbitrary weighting — see ADR-3.\n205\t- **Never guess an unmatched CPU's score.** A NULL/unscored state is always more honest than an estimate that could be wrong in either direction — see Benchmark Strategy.\n206\t- **Never read-modify-write a growing R2 file.** No real locking on object storage, and it gets slower and riskier as the file grows — see the v2 history storage pattern and Pipeline Run Lifecycle.\n207\t- **No client-side join or benchmark lookup.** The client only filters/sorts a pre-joined column; reintroducing a lookup in the browser undoes the entire point of precomputing the join server-side — see What It Is NOT.\n208\t- **No live kubectl mutation of the pipeline Deployment.** All changes go through `declarative-config` + ArgoCD, matching the standing house rule — a live edit just gets reverted by selfHeal anyway.\n209\t- **Never abort an entire run over one malformed listing.** Skip and log it instead — one bad record shouldn't cost every other listing in the run its data — see Failure Modes & Resilience.\n210\t\n211\t### Rollback & Safe Defaults\n212\t\n213\tThe safe default for any pipeline run failure, at any step, is to do nothing to the live snapshot and simply try again next cycle. There's no separate rollback command to define, because the design never lets a bad run become visible in the first place (Pipeline Run Lifecycle's verify-then-swap gate) — the previously published snapshot IS the rollback state, always, by construction. Nothing about this system requires manual intervention to recover from a single failed run.\n214\t\n215\t### Graceful Degradation / Offline Mode\n216\t\n217\tTwo distinct \"something's wrong\" states the client can be in, and what the user sees for each:\n218\t\n219\t- **Parquet fails to load in-browser** (network error, CORS misconfiguration, DuckDB-WASM init failure): an explicit error state naming the likely cause (e.g. \"Could not load auction data — check your connection and reload\"), never a blank page or silent hang — see Scenario 3.\n220\t- **Pipeline has stopped updating, but the last snapshot still loads fine**: the dashboard loads and works normally; the existing staleness indicator driven by `fetched_at` (see Client Dashboard Scope) is what surfaces this — no separate \"pipeline down\" banner needed, since a stale-but-correct snapshot degrades gracefully on its own.\n221\t\n222\t## Client Dashboard Scope (v1)\n223\t\n224\tSearch/filter/sort only, over the current snapshot — no history, no alerts, no comparison view, no auto-buy. These are all proven features elsewhere (see `docs/research/existing-tools.md`) that can be layered on later without changing the core architecture; v1 stays scoped to nailing the benchmark join and a clean filter/sort experience on top of it.\n225\t\n226\t- Filters: price (`price_effective_monthly`, not `price_base` — consistent with the value-focused framing used throughout this doc, see Data Models), RAM, disk type/size, uplink speed, CPU model, location/datacenter, ECC, benchmark-matched-only toggle.\n227\t- Sorts: any column, including all four per-resource value metrics independently (not just price) — `price_per_benchmark_point_single`, `price_per_benchmark_point_multi`, `price_per_gb_ram`, `price_per_tb_disk`.\n228\t- Default sort: `price_per_benchmark_point_multi` ascending, `NULLS FIRST` — multi-thread is the default because most Hetzner auction hardware is multi-core server-class and PassMark's own primary CPU Mark rating is multi-thread-based; `price_per_benchmark_point_single` remains an equally first-class, independently sortable column for buyers who weight single-core workloads more (see ADR-3). NULLS FIRST reinforces that benchmark-adjusted value, not raw price, is the point, and puts unscored listings (NULL `price_per_benchmark_point_multi`) at the top of the results instead of the bottom, keeping benchmark-map coverage gaps visible rather than easy to miss.\n229\t- Staleness indicator driven by `fetched_at`.\n230\t\n231\t### Performance Ceiling\n232\t\n233\t`docs/research/existing-tools.md` doesn't record an exact figure for how many listings Hetzner's Server Auction carries at any one time, so there's no verified data volume to size against yet. `[FILL IN once real listing-count data is observed from the pipeline's first few weeks of runs]` — the design should comfortably handle at least that scale, since DuckDB-WASM's range-request model only fetches the row groups a query touches rather than the whole file. If Hetzner's auction volume (or this schema's width) ever grows past what a single flat Parquet file can serve responsively client-side, the fallback is server-side pre-aggregation (a thin API doing the heavy filtering before the client sees rows) or narrower default filters on initial load — not a rearchitecture of the \"no backend at request time\" design.\n234\t\n235\t## v1.1 — Adopted Idea-Gen Additions\n236\t\n237\tNot part of v1's Phase 5 completion gate — adopted from the 2026-08-02 idea-gen run (full ledger and every considered/killed alternative: `docs/notes/ideas-ledger.md`) as near-term, non-blocking additions once v1 ships. Kept as a separate tier so Phase 5's gate stays exactly what it already is.\n238\t\n239\t- **Starter configs** (`had-4ct`). 3-5 pre-built example searches (e.g. \"Budget web server,\" \"Home NAS,\" \"Game server\") as one-click filter presets, for a visitor who doesn't want to configure filters from scratch.\n240\t- **One-click \"best deal now\" button** (`had-6a5f`). A single button returning one defensible top-value listing (highest `price_per_benchmark_point_multi` among `benchmark_matched = true` listings). Split from Starter configs — same finalist origin, separable feature.\n241\t- **User-selectable primary sort axis** (`had-1vp`). Let RAM- or storage-heavy buyers promote `price_per_gb_ram` or `price_per_tb_disk` to the primary sort instead of `price_per_benchmark_point_multi` — a direct, opt-in extension of ADR-3's \"separate metrics, user decides priority\" stance; the benchmark-value default (Client Dashboard Scope) doesn't change.\n242\t- **Diff view between two snapshots** (`had-33l`). Client-side (IndexedDB) comparison of \"what changed since I last looked\" — cache the previous fetched snapshot, diff row-by-config-signature against the current one. Gets partial price-history value weeks before v2's full historical-stats architecture ships, with zero pipeline changes.\n243\t- **Cross-link to Hetzner's own Cloud catalog pricing** (`had-39b`). Show \"X% cheaper than the equivalent still-selling Hetzner Cloud instance\" on each listing, using the small hand-maintained lookup table noted in Components.\n244\t- **Saved/named filter presets, URL-encoded** (`had-2ua`). Serialize filter state into URL query params on every change, read back on load — bookmarkable, no sharing required. **Deprioritized behind the four items above** — build last within this tier.\n245\t\n246\tTracked as beads in this repo's `.beads/` workspace (prefix `had`).\n247\t\n248\t## Testing Strategy\n249\t\n250\t- **CPU-matching fixture set.** A curated set of real Hetzner auction CPU strings, covering three distinct categories: (1) known-tricky *same-chip* variants that must all resolve to one correct match (e.g. \"Xeon E5-2680 v4\" vs. \"E5-2680v4\", differing whitespace/casing); (2) intentionally-unmatchable strings (e.g. a family with no benchmark entry at all), asserted as explicit `benchmark_matched = false`; and (3) **near-miss adversarial pairs** — real, similarly-named but genuinely distinct CPU models (e.g. \"Xeon E5-2680 v3\" vs. \"Xeon E5-2680 v4,\" same model number, different generation) — each asserted against its own correct match and asserted to *never* cross-match the other. Category (3) is the fixture set's only defense against Risk Register R1 (false-positive matches): categories (1) and (2) only prove the matcher finds the right answer or honestly gives up, neither proves it doesn't confidently produce the *wrong* one. This is the project's core heuristic logic (see Benchmark Strategy), so it's the one place this kind of test pays for itself; everywhere else in this project is comparatively low-risk.\n251\t- **Parquet/DuckDB-WASM conformance test.** Before Phase 3 is considered complete, a round-trip test writes a sample Parquet file with the pipeline's chosen writer and confirms DuckDB-WASM can actually load and query it via httpfs range requests — the one hand-off point between the two halves of the architecture where \"should work in theory\" isn't good enough. Gated at Phase 3, not later, so neither Phase 4's R2 publish infrastructure nor Phase 5's client UI gets built on top of an unverified file format.\n252\t- **Definition of done.** Before considering the pipeline or client phase complete: the CPU-matching fixture suite and the Parquet/DuckDB-WASM conformance test both pass. No CI-gated benchmark infrastructure beyond that — this is a solo hobby project, not a system with a regression budget to enforce.\n253\t\n254\t## Security\n255\t\n256\tProportionate to what this actually is — a personal dashboard with no user accounts, no PII, and no external users.\n257\t\n258\t- **Threat model:** none, explicitly. There are no external users, no authentication, and no PII anywhere in the system. The only credential in the whole project is the R2 API token, scoped to the bucket (not per-object) — that scope is what lets the same token publish both the Parquet snapshot and the `unmatched-cpus.json` report to it, via the temp-key-then-swap lifecycle (see Pipeline Run Lifecycle).\n259\t- **Secrets handling:** the R2 token is stored as an OpenBao-backed ExternalSecret (matching existing patterns in this environment), never logged by the pipeline, and rotated on the same ad-hoc cadence as other tokens in this environment — no fixed rotation schedule needed for a personal tool.\n260\t- **Untrusted input:** Hetzner's auction feed is the one piece of external input this system consumes. Parse it defensively — a malformed field on a single listing gets that listing skipped and logged (see Failure Modes & Resilience), never a crash of the whole run.\n261\t- **Supply chain:** pin the Anti-Patterns Catalog\n\nConsolidating the \"deliberately do not\" decisions already scattered through this plan into one place:\n\n- **No blended benchmark score.** Hides the number that matters most behind an arbitrary weighting — see ADR-3.\n- **Never guess an unmatched CPU's score.** A NULL/unscored state is always more honest than an estimate that could be wrong in either direction — see Benchmark Strategy.\n- **Never read-modify-write a growing R2 file.** No real locking on object storage, and it gets slower and riskier as the file grows — see the v2 history storage pattern and Pipeline Run Lifecycle.\n- **No client-side join or benchmark lookup.** The client only filters/sorts a pre-joined column; reintroducing a lookup in the browser undoes the entire point of precomputing the join server-side — see What It Is NOT.\n- **No live kubectl mutation of the pipeline Deployment.** All changes go through `declarative-config` + ArgoCD, matching the standing house rule — a live edit just gets reverted by selfHeal anyway.\n- **Never abort an entire run over one malformed listing.** Skip and log it instead — one bad record shouldn't cost every other listing in the run its data — see Failure Modes & Resilience.\n\n### Rollback & Safe Defaults\n\nThe safe default for any pipeline run failure, at any step, is to do nothing to the live snapshot and simply try again next cycle. There's no separate rollback command to define, because the design never lets a bad run become visible in the first place (Pipeline Run Lifecycle's verify-then-swap gate) — the previously published snapshot IS the rollback state, always, by construction. Nothing about this system requires manual intervention to recover from a single failed run.\n\n### Graceful Degradation / Offline Mode\n\nTwo distinct \"something's wrong\" states the client can be in, and what the user sees for each:\n\n- **Parquet fails to load in-browser** (network error, CORS misconfiguration, DuckDB-WASM init failure): an explicit error state naming the likely cause (e.g. \"Could not load auction data — check your connection and reload\"), never a blank page or silent hang — see Scenario 3.\n- **Pipeline has stopped updating, but the last snapshot still loads fine**: the dashboard loads and works normally; the existing staleness indicator driven by `fetched_at` (see Client Dashboard Scope) is what surfaces this — no separate \"pipeline down\" banner needed, since a stale-but-correct snapshot degrades gracefully on its own.\n\n## Client Dashboard Scope (v1)\n\nSearch/filter/sort only, over the current snapshot — no history, no alerts, no comparison view, no auto-buy. These are all proven features elsewhere (see `docs/research/existing-tools.md`) that can be layered on later without changing the core architecture; v1 stays scoped to nailing the benchmark join and a clean filter/sort experience on top of it.\n\n- Filters: price (`price_effective_monthly`, not `price_base` — consistent with the value-focused framing used throughout this doc, see Data Models), RAM, disk type/size, uplink speed, CPU model, location/datacenter, ECC, benchmark-matched-only toggle.\n- Sorts: any column, including all four per-resource value metrics independently (not just price) — `price_per_benchmark_point_single`, `price_per_benchmark_point_multi`, `price_per_gb_ram`, `price_per_tb_disk`.\n- Default sort: `price_per_benchmark_point_multi` ascending, `NULLS FIRST` — multi-thread is the default because most Hetzner auction hardware is multi-core server-class and PassMark's own primary CPU Mark rating is multi-thread-based; `price_per_benchmark_point_single` remains an equally first-class, independently sortable column for buyers who weight single-core workloads more (see ADR-3). NULLS FIRST reinforces that benchmark-adjusted value, not raw price, is the point, and puts unscored listings (NULL `price_per_benchmark_point_multi`) at the top of the results instead of the bottom, keeping benchmark-map coverage gaps visible rather than easy to miss.\n- Staleness indicator driven by `fetched_at`.\n\n### Performance Ceiling\n\n`docs/research/existing-tools.md` doesn't record an exact figure for how many listings Hetzner's Server Auction carries at any one time, so there's no verified data volume to size against yet. `[FILL IN once real listing-count data is observed from the pipeline's first few weeks of runs]` — the design should comfortably handle at least that scale, since DuckDB-WASM's range-request model only fetches the row groups a query touches rather than the whole file. If Hetzner's auction volume (or this schema's width) ever grows past what a single flat Parquet file can serve responsively client-side, the fallback is server-side pre-aggregation (a thin API doing the heavy filtering before the client sees rows) or narrower default filters on initial load — not a rearchitecture of the \"no backend at request time\" design.\n\n## v1.1 — Adopted Idea-Gen Additions\n\nNot part of v1's Phase 5 completion gate — adopted from the 2026-08-02 idea-gen run (full ledger and every considered/killed alternative: `docs/notes/ideas-ledger.md`) as near-term, non-blocking additions once v1 ships. Kept as a separate tier so Phase 5's gate stays exactly what it already is.\n\n- **Starter configs** (`had-4ct`). 3-5 pre-built example searches (e.g. \"Budget web server,\" \"Home NAS,\" \"Game server\") as one-click filter presets, for a visitor who doesn't want to configure filters from scratch.\n- **One-click \"best deal now\" button** (`had-6a5f`). A single button returning one defensible top-value listing (highest `price_per_benchmark_point_multi` among `benchmark_matched = true` listings). Split from Starter configs — same finalist origin, separable feature.\n- **User-selectable primary sort axis** (`had-1vp`). Let RAM- or storage-heavy buyers promote `price_per_gb_ram` or `price_per_tb_disk` to the primary sort instead of `price_per_benchmark_point_multi` — a direct, opt-in extension of ADR-3's \"separate metrics, user decides priority\" stance; the benchmark-value default (Client Dashboard Scope) doesn't change.\n- **Diff view between two snapshots** (`had-33l`). Client-side (IndexedDB) comparison of \"what changed since I last looked\" — cache the previous fetched snapshot, diff row-by-config-signature against the current one. Gets partial price-history value weeks before v2's full historical-stats architecture ships, with zero pipeline changes.\n- **Cross-link to Hetzner's own Cloud catalog pricing** (`had-39b`). Show \"X% cheaper than the equivalent still-selling Hetzner Cloud instance\" on each listing, using the small hand-maintained lookup table noted in Components.\n- **Saved/named filter presets, URL-encoded** (`had-2ua`). Serialize filter state into URL query params on every change, read back on load — bookmarkable, no sharing required. **Deprioritized behind the four items above** — build last within this tier.\n\nTracked as beads in this repo's `.beads/` workspace (prefix `had`).\n\n## Testing Strategy\n\n- **CPU-matching fixture set.** A curated set of real Hetzner auction CPU strings, covering three distinct categories: (1) known-tricky *same-chip* variants that must all resolve to one correct match (e.g. \"Xeon E5-2680 v4\" vs. \"E5-2680v4\", differing whitespace/casing); (2) intentionally-unmatchable strings (e.g. a family with no benchmark entry at all), asserted as explicit `benchmark_matched = false`; and (3) **near-miss adversarial pairs** — real, similarly-named but genuinely distinct CPU models (e.g. \"Xeon E5-2680 v3\" vs. \"Xeon E5-2680 v4,\" same model number, different generation) — each asserted against its own correct match and asserted to *never* cross-match the other. Category (3) is the fixture set's only defense against Risk Register R1 (false-positive matches): categories (1) and (2) only prove the matcher finds the right answer or honestly gives up, neither proves it doesn't confidently produce the *wrong* one. This is the project's core heuristic logic (see Benchmark Strategy), so it's the one place this kind of test pays for itself; everywhere else in this project is comparatively low-risk.\n- **Parquet/DuckDB-WASM conformance test.** Before Phase 3 is considered complete, a round-trip test writes a sample Parquet file with the pipeline's chosen writer and confirms DuckDB-WASM can actually load and query it via httpfs range requests — the one hand-off point between the two halves of the architecture where \"should work in theory\" isn't good enough. Gated at Phase 3, not later, so neither Phase 4's R2 publish infrastructure nor Phase 5's client UI gets built on top of an unverified file format.\n- **Definition of done.** Before considering the pipeline or client phase complete: the CPU-matching fixture suite and the Parquet/DuckDB-WASM conformance test both pass. No CI-gated benchmark infrastructure beyond that — this is a solo hobby project, not a system with a regression budget to enforce.\n\n## Security\n\nProportionate to what this actually is — a personal dashboard with no user accounts, no PII, and no external users.\n\n- **Threat model:** none, explicitly. There are no external users, no authentication, and no PII anywhere in the system. The only credential in the whole project is the R2 API token, scoped to the bucket (not per-object) — that scope is what lets the same token publish both the Parquet snapshot and the `unmatched-cpus.json` report to it, via the temp-key-then-swap lifecycle (see Pipeline Run Lifecycle).\n- **Secrets handling:** the R2 token is stored as an OpenBao-backed ExternalSecret (matching existing patterns in this environment), never logged by the pipeline, and rotated on the same ad-hoc cadence as other tokens in this environment — no fixed rotation schedule needed for a personal tool.\n- **Untrusted input:** Hetzner's auction feed is the one piece of external input this system consumes. Parse it defensively — a malformed field on a single listing gets that listing skipped and logged (see Failure Modes & Resilience), never a crash of the whole run.\n- **Supply chain:** pin the DuckDB-WASM version and pipeline library versions explicitly; no `:latest` image tags on the pipeline container, matching the house rule already in place for this environment.\n\nExplicitly out of scope at this scale: audit logging and a per-threat security matrix — there's no security boundary here worth building either for.\n\n## Implementation Phases\n\n- [ ] **Phase 1: Pipeline — fetch Hetzner auction data, define raw schema**\n  Delivers: a working fetcher against Hetzner's live auction feed and a defined raw schema for what a listing looks like before any enrichment.\n  Completion criteria:\n  - Each preset defines a specific use case with optimized filter criteria and sorting.\n\n## Current Presets\n\n### 1. Budget Web Server 🌐\n- **Use case**: Affordable web hosting and light workloads\n- **Filters**: Max €30/month, 16GB+ RAM, benchmark-matched only\n- **Sort**: Value (multi-thread benchmark)\n\n### 2. Home NAS 💾\n- **Use case**: File server, backup, or media storage\n- **Filters**: Max €50/month, 8GB+ RAM, 4TB+ HDD storage\n- **Sort**: Value per TB disk\n\n### 3. Game Server 🎮\n- **Use case**: High single-thread performance for game hosting\n- **Filters**: Max €60/month, 32GB+ RAM, Ryzen CPU, NVMe storage\n- **Sort**: Value (single-thread benchmark)\n\n### 4. Compute Intensive ⚡\n- **Use case**: Rendering, scientific computing, batch processing\n- **Filters**: Max €80/month, 64GB+ RAM, benchmark-matched only\n- **Sort**: Value (multi-thread benchmark)\n\n### 5. Storage Focused 📦\n- **Use case**: Bulk storage, backups, archives\n- **Filters**: Max €40/month, 16GB+ RAM, 2TB+ HDD storage\n- **Sort**: Value per TB disk\n\n## File Structure\n\n```\nweb/\n├── index.html              # Main dashboard with starter config UI\n├── starter-configs.json    # Preset definitions (loaded in production)\n└── README.md              # This documentation\n```\n\n## Adding New Presets\n\nTo add a new preset:\n\n1. **Edit `starter-configs.json`** (or the `starterConfigs` object in `index.html` for development):\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"your-new-preset\",\n  \"name\": \"Your New Preset\",\n  \"description\": \"Brief description of the use case\",\n  \"icon\": \"🎯\",\n  \"filters\": {\n    \"price_effective_monthly_max\": 100,\n    \"ram_gb_min\": 32,\n    \"cpu_family_preference\": \"any\",\n    \"disk_type\": \"any\",\n    \"benchmark_matched_only\": true\n  },\n  \"sort\": \"price_per_benchmark_point_multi\",\n  \"sort_direction\": \"asc\"\n}\n```\n\n2. **Filter Options**:\n   - `price_effective_monthly_max`: Maximum monthly price (€)\n   - `ram_gb_min`: Minimum RAM (GB)\n   - `cpu_family_preference`: \"any\", \"ryzen\", \"xeon\", or \"core\"\n   - `disk_type`: \"any\", \"nvme\", \"ssd\", or \"hdd\"\n   - `disk_size_tb_min`: Minimum total disk size (TB)\n   - `benchmark_matched_only`: true/false\n\n3. **Sort Options**:\n   - `price_per_benchmark_point_multi`: Value per multi-thread benchmark\n   - `price_per_benchmark_point_single`: Value per single-thread benchmark\n   - `price_per_gb_ram`: Value per GB RAM\n   - `price_per_tb_disk`: Value per TB disk\n\n4. **Sort Direction**: \"asc\" (ascending) or \"desc\" (descending)\n\n## Integration with DuckDB-WASM\n\nThe current implementation uses mock data for demonstration. In production:\n\n1. The `starter-configs.json` file will be loaded via `fetch()`\n2. Listings data will come from DuckDB-WASM querying the Parquet file\n3. Filter logic will be converted to SQL WHERE clauses\n4. Sort logic will be converted to SQL ORDER BY clauses\n\nExample SQL integration:\n\n```sql\nSELECT * FROM auction_listings\nWHERE price_effective_monthly <= {max_price}\n  AND ram_gb >= {min_ram}\n  AND benchmark_matched = {matched_only}\nORDER BY {sort_column} {sort_direction}\nLIMIT 100\n```\n\n## User Experience\n\n1. **One-click application**: Users click a preset card to apply all filters and sorting instantly\n2. **Visual feedback**: Active preset is highlighted with a blue border\n3. **Manual override**: Users can manually adjust filters after selecting a preset\n4. **Clear indication**: Preset selection is cleared when filters are manually modified\n\n## Future Enhancements\n\nPotential improvements for v1.1+:\n\n- **Custom presets**: Allow users to save their own filter combinations\n- **URL encoding**: Bookmarkable preset links (see bead `had-2ua`)\n- **A/B testing**: Track which presets are most used\n- **Dynamic recommendations**: Suggest presets based on user behavior\n- **Preset categories**: Group presets by workload type\n\n## Bead Tracking\n\nThis implementation corresponds to bead `had-4ct` from the 2026-08-02 idea-gen run.\n\nSee `docs/notes/ideas-ledger.md` for the full context of how this feature was prioritized and selected.\n"}}],"stop_reason":null,"stop_sequence":null,"usage":{"input_tokens":0,"output_tokens":0},"context_management":null},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"ceb9ea6b-b897-4622-86c4-1b6f6e157691","uuid":"44e4fc33-2e84-422f-bf7e-6e82155adf7b","timestamp":"2026-08-02T15:12:35.565Z"}
